topic: The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM): how it works, implementation timeline and international political reactions

key_points.point: CBAM puts a carbon price on imports of cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen to counter carbon leakage; importers buy and surrender certificates matching embedded emissions.
Certificate prices track EU ETS allowance auction prices: quarterly averages in 2026, weekly averages from 2027.
The reporting-only transitional period ran from 1 October 2023 to end-2025; the definitive regime with financial obligations began on 1 January 2026.
The Omnibus simplification (in force 20 October 2025) replaced the EUR 150 exemption with a 50-tonne annual per-importer threshold; importers above it need authorised declarant status.
Certificate sales start 1 February 2027 for 2026 imports, and the first annual declaration and surrender is due 30 September 2027 (moved from 31 May).
CBAM phases in as EU ETS free allocation is phased out; the 2026 and 2027 CBAM factors are 97.5% and 95%, reaching zero free allocation in 2034 under current law.
Carbon prices paid in the country of origin can be deducted if verified, and default emissions values apply where actual data are lacking.
The Commission has proposed extending CBAM to about 180 downstream steel and aluminium products from 2028 and anti-circumvention measures; these were proposals, not adopted law.
On 17 July 2026 the Commission proposed (COM(2026) 616) slowing the free allocation phase-out to 2038; still under negotiation, it would raise importer obligations from 2028.
China, India, South Africa and Russia criticise CBAM as unfair or discriminatory; Russia filed a WTO case in 2025 and Poland challenged CBAM at the EU Court of Justice.
At COP30 governments agreed only to trade-and-climate dialogues over three years after references to unilateral trade measures were downgraded; the EU rejects that label for CBAM.
The India-EU FTA gave India no CBAM exemption but a dedicated annexure and work plan, with a clause extending any future EU CBAM flexibility to India (per an Indian official).
